stem: A 55-year-old man presents with hematemesis and melena. Endoscopy reveals a submucosal gastric mass, and biopsy shows tumor cells positive for c-KIT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: A submucosal gastric mass that is c-KIT (CD117) positive on immunohistochemistry = gastrointestinal stromal tumour. GISTs are submucosal, often present with bleeding (haematemesis/melena) and are c-KIT positive in ~95%.

why.B: Adenocarcinoma arises from the mucosa (an ulcer/mass seen on the surface) and is c-KIT negative.
why.C: Leiomyoma is submucosal too, but it is desmin/SMA positive and c-KIT negative.
why.D: An ulcer is not a mass, and its biopsy shows no tumour cells.

stem: A 58-year-old male presents with early satiety and vague abdominal discomfort. CT scan shows a 6 cm gastric mass arising from the stomach wall. Biopsy confirms a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) without evidence of metastasis. What is the most appropriate management?
srcNote: Source note (Final 441 F Q25): In the GIST >2 cm procedure-choice version, the source marks C. Wedge resection with a check mark.
expl: Localized GIST > 2 cm → surgical resection with negative (R0) margins — a wedge/segmental resection is enough. GISTs rarely spread to lymph nodes, so no lymphadenectomy; imatinib is added for high-risk or unresectable disease.

why.A: Classic chemotherapy doesn't work for GIST (the targeted drug is imatinib, an adjunct).
why.C: Correct — complete resection with clear margins (the source's version marks wedge resection).
why.D: Endoscopic mucosal resection is for mucosal lesions (early adenocarcinoma); a 6-cm GIST arises deep in the muscularis propria.

stem: GIST is associated with which type of mutation?
ansText: c-KIT (CD117) — a tyrosine-kinase receptor mutation (~95% of GISTs; target of imatinib). A minority have PDGFRA mutations. DOG-1 is another diagnostic marker.

stem: 68y male with non-bilious recurrent vomiting of undigested food. Lost 13 kg in 3 months and he was cashetic and pale. What diagnosis ?
srcNote: (Esophageal tumor & esophageal disorders) Source note (Final 439 F Q18): The related recall supplies only one option: A. Gastric cancer obstruction. Ans:A.
expl: Recurrent non-bilious vomiting of undigested food (food stays in the stomach), major weight loss and cachexia in an elderly man = gastric outlet obstruction, most likely from distal gastric (antral) cancer. Non-bilious means the block is proximal to the ampulla.

why.A: GERD causes heartburn/regurgitation, not vomiting of undigested food with 13 kg weight loss.
why.B: Gastritis causes dyspepsia, not outlet obstruction or cachexia.
why.C: Correct — obstructed gastric outlet (from gastric cancer).
why.D: A duodenal ulcer can scar the pylorus and obstruct it, but the age, cachexia and pallor point to malignancy; "obstructed gastric outlet" describes the presentation.

stem: A 69-year-old man presented with a history of epigastric vague pain for two months associated with loss of weight (15kg). Physical examination was normal. Abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography were normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
expl: An elderly man with epigastric pain and 15 kg weight loss has alarm features → upper GI endoscopy with biopsy, even though US and CT were normal (CT misses mucosal lesions).

why.A: MRI adds nothing over a normal CT for mucosal disease.
why.B: Diagnostic laparoscopy is a staging tool after a cancer is diagnosed.
why.D: A contrast follow-through looks at the small bowel and cannot biopsy.

srcNote: Incomplete choice set: only 2 options are supplied in the source.
expl: GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal — the pacemaker cells of the GI tract.

why.B: Squamous cells give squamous cell carcinoma (e.g. oesophagus), not GIST.

stem: A 57 years old man presents with epigastric pain CT shows a mass with calcification. Levels of ”hydroxy indole acetic acid” was high. What is the tumor?
expl: High urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), the serotonin breakdown product, = carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumour; carcinoid masses can calcify.

why.B: GIST does not secrete serotonin (it is c-KIT positive).
why.C: Schwannomas are nerve-sheath tumours, not secretory.

stem: someone who had MALTOMA and evidence of H.pylori infection what is the Treatment?
expl: Low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma is driven by H. pylori — eradication antibiotics (triple therapy) are first-line and make most tumours regress.

why.B: Chemotherapy is for high-grade disease or failure of eradication.
why.C: Radiotherapy is used when the lymphoma persists after eradication or is H. pylori negative.
why.D: Surgery is rarely needed (complications such as perforation or bleeding).

stem: A 62 y.o male presented to OPD C/O early satiety and wt. loss (11kg) for the last 3 months. Physical examination was unremarkable. Upper GI endoscopy with multiple biopsies has been taken: Histopathology:gastric adenocarcinoma, Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
expl: Once biopsy confirms gastric adenocarcinoma, stage it. The first step is CT chest/abdomen/pelvis to look for distant metastasis. EUS (T stage of early lesions) and diagnostic laparoscopy (occult peritoneal disease) come after the CT.

why.A: EUS is useful but comes after CT shows no metastasis.
why.C: Laparoscopy is for ≥ T1b disease after CT shows no metastasis.
why.D: MRI isn't the routine staging study.

stem: Which of the following organism carries the risk of upper gastrointestinal neoplastic diseases?
srcNote: ( Acute abdomen ) Source note (Midterm 429 F Q52): Helicobacter pylori is the commonest cause of peptic ulceration and gastric adenocarcinoma world wide. Reference: Davidson 6th ed. ch. 13 p. 171
expl: H. pylori is the commonest cause of peptic ulceration and gastric adenocarcinoma worldwide (also MALT lymphoma) — chronic inflammation → mutations.

why.A: C. perfringens causes gas gangrene and food poisoning.
why.B: S. pyogenes causes pharyngitis, cellulitis and necrotising fasciitis.
why.C: S. aureus causes skin and wound infections — not neoplasia.

stem: A 65 y\o man, presented to outpatient clinic complaining of epigastric pain and early satiety for 3 months. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed antral gastric mass. Confirmed by biopsy and histopathology to be adenocarcinoma. Patient was consented for surgery.Which of the following low blood level is suggestive of nutritional deficiency?
expl: Serum albumin is the standard laboratory marker of nutritional status before surgery — a low level (< 3.5 g/dL, or < 3.0 g/dL as severe) predicts more complications and poor healing.

why.B: Magnesium is an electrolyte, not a nutritional marker.
why.C: Transferrin (and prealbumin) also reflect nutrition, but albumin is the classic answer; transferrin also rises with iron deficiency, so it isn't reliable here.
why.D: Low iron in gastric cancer mostly reflects chronic blood loss, not general nutrition.
